structure.title: Chapters 1–16 · Grand Isle
structure.text: At a summer resort Edna's days seem to belong to her husband, children and fellow guests in roughly equal shares. A piano performance and a night swim give her experiences whose importance she would find difficult to explain to anyone waiting on shore.

structure.title: Chapters 17–25 · New Orleans
structure.text: At home Léonce measures prosperity by the furnishings of his house and by who calls there. Edna stops receiving callers and devotes time to painting. Her refusal of a weekly duty gives her husband something definite to complain about and herself the alarming pleasure of an afternoon of her own.

structure.title: Chapters 26–39 · A house within walking distance
structure.text: Edna seeks a smaller place whose expenses she can meet. It seems possible to choose one's furniture, one's guests and the hour one comes home. The people she desires and the children who depend on her complicate that new arithmetic.

people.name: Edna Pontellier
people.text: Her new desires arrive partly through bodily skill. She can do something in the water that frightened her yesterday. Painting makes a different demand. It matters whether she will give it time even when nobody is particularly pleased with the picture.

people.name: Adèle Ratignolle and Mademoiselle Reisz
people.text: Adèle makes affection look easy and motherhood beautiful. The pianist lives alone and has little interest in being agreeable. Edna finds pleasure in both women's company and scant reason to think she could borrow either life entire.

context.title: Frank talk, strict expectations
context.text: Edna is an outsider among the Creole families at Grand Isle. Their ease with intimate conversation can startle her. The same people who joke freely about a married woman's admirers may have quite settled expectations about what she will do.

notice.text: Notice who makes free time possible.
notice.why: A nursemaid accompanies the children and servants keep the houses going. Every hour Edna can spend painting or alone by the water rests on arrangements another woman may experience as work.

notice.text: Hear what passes between people at the piano.
notice.why: A conventional performance can supply pictures Edna already knows how to imagine. Reisz's playing leaves her shaken before she can name what she has felt. Chopin returns to that interval between bodily knowledge and explanation.

opening: Edna Pontellier has a husband, children, and a comfortable place in New Orleans society. During a summer by the sea, she begins wanting things that cannot be fitted neatly around them. Swimming, music, and another man's attention make her feel that a life she had accepted might be only one possibility. Kate Chopin follows the discovery into ordinary arrangements about houses, money, and duty, where a woman's desire for a life of her own becomes everyone else's problem to explain away.
